title: Accept Uncertainty for Job Satisfaction, Says Study
paragraphs: Many people feel pressure to choose the perfect job or make the perfect career decision. But according to a new study, accepting that some uncertainty is unavoidable may actually lead to a more satisfying working life.

The study was led by Hui Xu of the University of Macau, together with Blake Allan of the University of Houston. It was published in July in the Journal of Counseling Psychology, a journal of the American Psychological Association.

The researchers focused on something called "career wisdom." This is the ability to make career decisions when there is no obvious right answer. It involves gathering information, accepting that some uncertainty will always remain, trusting your instincts, and moving forward even when you feel uncomfortable. Unlike personality traits, career wisdom is something that can be developed through education and counseling.

To study its effects, the researchers followed 995 employed adults in the United States for six months. At the beginning of the study, participants answered questions to measure their career wisdom. Three months later, they reported how meaningful they found their work. After another three months, they reported their levels of job satisfaction, life satisfaction and engagement at work.

The results showed that people with more career wisdom at the start were more likely to find their work meaningful three months later. In turn, people who found their work more meaningful reported higher job satisfaction and engagement after another three months. The connection with overall life satisfaction was weaker. These patterns were similar regardless of gender, race or economic background.

Xu said that career counseling may need to do more than help people collect information and make logical plans, since people also need help dealing with the uncertainty that remains. However, Xu stressed that career wisdom does not mean making random or impulsive decisions. Instead, it means balancing careful problem-solving with the willingness to move forward when certainty is impossible.
The researchers noted that the study was observational, so it cannot prove that career wisdom directly causes greater satisfaction. All of the data was also based on participants' own reports.
